paragraphs.heading: A formula for each unknown
paragraphs.text: Cramer's rule is an explicit formula that solves a system of linear equations having as many equations as unknowns, whenever that system has exactly one solution. It writes each unknown using determinants: one of the square coefficient matrix A, and one of a matrix Aᵢ made by swapping the i-th column of A for the column b of right-hand sides.

paragraphs.heading: What a determinant measures
paragraphs.text: Geometrically, the determinant of n vectors of length n gives the volume of the slanted box, or parallelepiped, that those vectors span in n-dimensional space. This picture offers a way to see why the rule works, and the argument is not limited to two equations in two unknowns.

paragraphs.heading: Who it is named after
paragraphs.text: The rule carries the name of Gabriel Cramer, who published it for any number of unknowns in 1750. Colin Maclaurin had already published special cases in 1748, and may have known it as early as 1729.

paragraphs.heading: Why it works
paragraphs.text: The proof leans on two facts about determinants. A determinant is linear in any single column, and it equals zero whenever two columns are the same. The rule also holds when the numbers come from any field, not only the real numbers. It even yields a formula for the inverse of A, as long as det(A) ≠ 0.

paragraphs.heading: When the determinant is zero
paragraphs.text: The rule needs the coefficient determinant to be nonzero. A system with no solutions is called inconsistent, and one with more than one solution is called indeterminate. For two equations in two unknowns with a zero coefficient determinant, nonzero numerator determinants mean the system is inconsistent, while zero ones mean it is indeterminate. For three or more unknowns, a nonzero numerator still means inconsistent, but all zeros proves nothing. The three equations x+y+z=1, x+y+z=2 and x+y+z=3 make every determinant vanish, yet they have no solution.

paragraphs.heading: Where it turns up
paragraphs.text: The method of variation of parameters relies on Cramer's rule to find the general solution of an inhomogeneous linear differential equation. It also proves that an integer programming problem with a totally unimodular constraint matrix and integer right-hand side has integer basic solutions, which makes such problems much easier. It can also show that the divergence operator on a Riemannian manifold does not change when coordinates change.
